questions.q: Kirchhoff's Current Law states that the sum of the currents flowing into a junction is equal in magnitude to the sum of the currents flowing out of that junction. Which conservation principle does this law express?
options: The conservation of energy
The conservation of charge, because charge cannot build up or disappear at a junction
The conservation of momentum
The conservation of mass
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Current Law (\(\Sigma I = 0\), or \(I_{in} = I_{out}\)) expresses the conservation of charge: electrons do not build up at a point in a conductor, so the current flowing into a junction must equal the current flowing out. Naming the conservation principle is the mark students forget.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that in any closed loop of a circuit, the sum of the voltage drops must equal the sum of the emfs in that loop. Which conservation principle does this law express?
options: The conservation of charge
The conservation of energy, because electrical energy must be conserved around a closed loop
The conservation of current
The conservation of resistance
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (\(\Sigma V = 0\) for any closed-circuit loop) expresses the conservation of energy: a unit of charge travelling around a loop must gain as much energy from the emfs as it loses in the voltage drops across the components.

questions.q: When resistors are connected in series there is only one path for the current to flow through. How is the effective resistance of resistors connected in series found?
options: By taking the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances
By obtaining the sum of the individual resistances, \(R_T = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)
By multiplying the individual resistances together
By averaging the individual resistances
questions.explanation: Because there is only one path, the same current flows through each resistor and the voltage drops add: \(V_T = I(R_1+R_2+R_3)\). Dividing by the current gives \(R_T = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\), so the resistance of a series circuit is greater than that of any individual resistor.

questions.q: Find the effective resistance of a circuit comprising three resistors, having resistance values of 15 Ω, 25 Ω and 34 Ω, connected in series.
working: For resistors in series the effective resistance is the sum of the individual resistances:
questions.explanation: In series the resistances simply add. The total, 74 Ω, is greater than any individual resistor, exactly as the series rule predicts.

questions.q: When resistors are connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the effective resistance is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances. How does the effective resistance compare with the individual resistances?
options: It is greater than the largest individual resistance
It is equal to the average of the individual resistances
It is less than the smallest individual resistance, because adding parallel paths makes it easier for current to flow
It is equal to the smallest individual resistance
questions.explanation: The effective resistance of resistors in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance. The more resistors added in parallel, the more paths there are for the current to flow through, so more current flows for the same voltage and the resistance is reduced.

questions.q: What is the effective resistance of three resistors connected in parallel if they have resistance values of 5.0 Ω, 10 Ω and 20 Ω respectively?
questions.explanation: Remember to take the reciprocal at the end: \(1/R_T = 7/20\) gives \(R_T = 20/7 = 2.9\,\Omega\), not \(7/20\). Note the effective resistance is less than the smallest resistor (5.0 Ω), as the parallel rule promises.

questions.q: From memory: when resistors are connected in series to a power supply, what is true about the current through each resistor, the voltage drops across the resistors, and the total resistance?
keyPoints: The same current passes through each resistor and through the power supply (only one path).
The sum of the voltage drops across the resistors equals the voltage rise across the power supply.
The effective resistance is the sum of the individual resistances, \(R_T = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\), so adding a resistor in series increases the total resistance.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three series rules — same current, voltage drops add to the supply, resistances add — grade yourself Good or Easy. Series: same current, voltage shares, resistances add.

questions.q: An advantage of having parallel circuits is that all appliances have the same voltage across them and the appliances can be switched on independently. Explain why these advantages arise, and describe what would happen instead if the appliances were connected in series. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: When appliances are connected in parallel, every appliance has the same voltage across it, equal to the supply voltage (230 V), regardless of what else is switched on, because each branch spans the same two points. If the appliances were instead connected in series they would share the supply voltage between them, so no appliance would receive the full voltage it was designed for. A second advantage is that each appliance can be switched on and off independently: each branch has its own path, so switching off (or the failure of) one branch does not break the others, whereas in a series circuit a single break stops the current everywhere and all appliances would be on or off together.

criteria.descriptor: States that in parallel each appliance receives the full supply voltage (e.g. 230 V).
States that appliances can be switched on/off independently because each has its own path.
Contrasts with series, where appliances share the voltage and a single break stops everything.

questions.explanation: Both advantages flow directly from the parallel rules: same voltage on every branch, and independent paths. The series comparison earns the third mark.

questions.q: Why does the largest resistor dissipate the most power in a series circuit, while the smallest resistor dissipates the most power in a parallel circuit?
options: Power does not depend on the configuration; the same resistor dissipates the most in both
In series the same current flows, so \(P = I^2R\) makes the largest resistance dominate; in parallel the same voltage acts, so \(P = V^2/R\) makes the smallest resistance dominate
In series the same voltage acts, so larger resistors draw more current; in parallel larger resistors draw more current
The largest resistor always dissipates the most power because it stores the most charge
questions.explanation: Match the power formula to the quantity that is constant. In series the current is shared (constant), so use \(P = I^2R\) — bigger \(R\), more power. In parallel the voltage is constant, so use \(P = V^2/R\) — smaller \(R\), more power. The reversal comes entirely from which quantity is shared.

questions.q: From memory: what single pair of facts lets you immediately tell whether a circuit is series or parallel, and what does each tell you about the other quantity?
keyPoints: In a series circuit the current is the same through every component (one path); the voltage divides.
In a parallel circuit the voltage is the same across every branch (each branch spans the same two points); the current divides.
Whichever quantity is 'the same' tells you the configuration; the other quantity is the one that divides. Lock it: series shares voltage, parallel shares current.
questions.explanation: This is the key to the whole topic. If you recalled 'series = same current, parallel = same voltage' and that the other quantity divides, grade yourself Good or Easy.
